source: CK-12 Life Science Concepts for Middle School, Section 11.1, CC-BY-NC
notes: Class B document (15 units). Sequential organ pathway lesson, uses a multinuclear Sequence relation for the digestive pathway. One ECU for stomach detail.

units.label: Hook: why do we need digestion (text)
units.content_summary: Food contains large complex molecules (proteins, carbohydrates, fats) that cells cannot use directly. Digestion breaks these down into small absorbable molecules (amino acids, simple sugars, fatty acids).

units.label: Learning Objectives (text)
units.content_summary: Objectives: list the main organs of the digestive system in order; describe the function of each organ; distinguish mechanical from chemical digestion.

units.label: Full digestive tract diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Full-body diagram showing the digestive tract: mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, with liver and pancreas as accessory organs.

units.label: Mouth: mechanical and chemical digestion (text)
units.content_summary: Mouth: teeth mechanically break food (chewing); saliva contains amylase enzyme beginning chemical breakdown of starches. Tongue shapes food into a bolus for swallowing.

units.label: Esophagus: peristalsis (text)
units.content_summary: Esophagus: muscular tube connecting mouth to stomach. Peristalsis (wave-like muscle contractions) pushes food down, working even upside down or in zero gravity.

units.label: Stomach: acid and enzyme digestion (text)
units.content_summary: Stomach churns food and secretes hydrochloric acid (pH~2) and pepsin enzyme, breaking down proteins. Mucus lining protects stomach walls from self-digestion. Food becomes a liquid called chyme.

units.label: Stomach cross-section diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Cross-section of the stomach wall showing mucus lining, acid-secreting cells, and the muscular layers responsible for churning.

units.label: Small intestine: nutrient absorption (text)
units.content_summary: Small intestine (~6m long): most digestion and nutrient absorption occurs here. Villi (finger-like projections) increase surface area for absorption. Enzymes from pancreas and bile from liver aid digestion here.

units.label: Villi diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Magnified diagram of intestinal villi showing blood vessels absorbing nutrients, with a zoomed inset showing microvilli increasing surface area further.

units.label: Large intestine: water absorption (text)
units.content_summary: Large intestine (~1.5m): absorbs remaining water and salts from indigestible material. Contains beneficial bacteria that produce some vitamins. Remaining waste becomes feces, stored in rectum until elimination.

units.label: Video: food's journey animation (video)
units.content_summary: Full animated journey of a bite of food through the entire digestive tract, showing mechanical and chemical changes at each organ in sequence.

units.label: Accessory organs: liver and pancreas (text)
units.content_summary: Liver produces bile (emulsifies fats) stored in the gallbladder. Pancreas produces digestive enzymes and bicarbonate to neutralize stomach acid entering the small intestine. Neither food passes through them directly.

units.label: Practice questions (text)
units.content_summary: Five questions: order the organs correctly; identify where protein digestion begins; explain the role of villi; describe two accessory organs and their functions.
